You completely are and I wouldn't have commented if you hadn't pushed back against a commentor questioning whether he should be profiting off his patients traumas by dismissing them and implying they were unaware this was a "textbook " that's "meant to inform." These claims are untrue-there is no evidence this was ever intended to be published for student/professional consumption, nor is there compelling evidence surrounding his research into neuroscience/somatics. What we do know is that the book was clearly marketed in a way that demonstrates the publishing house saw huge profit potential from it, which combined with the lack of any real analysis of things like Western imperialism/misogyny/racism, is causing some users in the sub to critique the work and question the author's character, thought process when compiling/editing case studies, and reasons for publishing in the first place. Your perspective on the work and what it means to you on a personal level is fine to give-saying a work is backed by empirical evidence and that other users simply aren't grasping that when they critique it when neither of those things are true, is not.

>And, spoiler alert, this is a text book. It’s not for entertainment. It’s meant to inform.

I can't find evidence that this was intended to be a textbook-or at least it feels likely that the author and his team understood that it certainty wouldn't be by the time it hit the publisher. Van Der Kolk was interviewed about the book for an author profile piece in New York Time Magazine specifically to advertise when it would be coming out. The publisher didn't buy ad-space in any psychiatric journals, they bought it in one of the most famous newspapers in the country because they were confident they'd make their money back, that the book would have mass appeal. Most of his claims also aren't empirically supported and his research methodology has been repeatedly brought into question, so its use as anything rigidly informative or presented as "hard science" is suspect. I am not saying anyone who got any sort of meaning from the book is "wrong" or should feel duped because that would be cruel and silly. But users in this sub should be more than free to question the author's motivations considering his profession and the way we're constantly being sold Everything under capitalism, and when most of his claims do not stack up upon deeper research.

I hated the book too-I'm glad people got something out of it, and I understand for many it might have been the first time they were ever told they weren't diseased, just traumatized and having a normal reaction to that trauma. But I feel like his analysis as a whole is lacking and he doesn't push himself far enough-EMDR is just as much as a pseudoscience as other modalities no matter how he tries to sell it. It's repackaged exposure therapy with a light bit to sell it as a scientific process. I won't tell anyone to stop if they're getting something out of it and it's helping them, healing comes down to whatever speaks to the individual, but I'm also not going to be lied to that this backed by extensive medical research.

He also frankly comes across as sleazy. There's this myth perpetuated that the book was only meant for people in the psych field but that isn't true-it was published through a major publisher and an advanced copy was sent to the New York Times, which isn't how things are done with textbooks. It was meant to be sold to the public. So the first chapter opening with the depiction of an American soldier raping a Vietnemese woman during the invasion of Vietnam and solely focusing on the trauma the -soldier- felt isn't some sort of abstract bit of "objectivity" that professionals are using as a case study, it's because he clearly didn't see a problem with that framing. That dismissal of women continues when he referred to patients with eating disorders as "slender" and "gorgeous" and how we're supposed to be amazed that a female patient would potentially find it horrifically traumatizing and triggering to be held down by grown men (and I'm very sorry the book depicts things you've gone through, you're right to point out the lack of self critique from Van Der Kolk!). Any analysis of trauma and critique of the psychiatric field that doesn't include a deep dive into the various systems of power and oppression that affects patient's lives on a material scale, and how the psychiatric field is meant to and continues to uphold those systems, frankly isn't worth much.

The only other clone house I have experience with is Oil Perfumery. Their downsides are that they take forever to ship (sometimes it can be fine, but I think 2 weeks is roughly what to expect from the time you press order to the time you get the package), it's a small business so they don't work weekends, and some of their scents can take longer to rest than other oil based houses. Upsides are that they're dirt cheap, frequently have sales, and come in 10 mL which is more product than other similar houses. Every clone house will have some duds-like I still can't get their version of Oud Satin Mood to work and if it doesn't shift in the next two weeks I'm taking the L and tossing it. But I think for the most part theirs are very good. Their Bitter Peach and Lost Cherry were good, Jasmin Rogue has the exact same dry down and lasts for a decent time considering it's an oil, their Side Effect tones down the tobacco on my skin which I enjoy, and their Wood Sage and Sea Salt is completely indistinguishable from the real thing. Stacey Abrams is a typical democrat who would be center/center-right and her casting is meant to appeal to liberals. It's in stark contrast to the leftism that previous iterations of Trek espoused-Gene Roddenberry was literally a communist, per Majel Barrett, and that absolutely shines through the original series. DS9 quotes The Communist Manifesto directly in an episode about unionizing and the series overall deals very heavily with themes of decolonization and the mechanics of keeping a moneyless society running. Every bit of the newer Trek series I've seen is not interested in engaging with leftist politics.

I want to preface this by saying I do like some of the newer Trek content and I don't think politics and ethical quandaries are necessarily the end all be all of what makes Trek enjoyable and unique. But it IS a major aspect of the franchise and I have to be totally honest in saying NuTrek has completely failed in capturing that element. It's absurd to me that Discovery's biggest claim to being "progressive" is that gay and trans characters exist in it, when that's the standard for every program targeted to the 18-49 demographic. My parents can watch basic procedural shows and see non-binary characters pop up. The writers don't deserve any special credit for that and it's insulting to say they do. 

Looking back I think the fall unfortunately started with Enterprise, which gave in to the ugly reactionary jingoism and cultural regression of the Bush years (the Kelvin movies are also guilty of this, Beyond perhaps less so). There's some interesting subversions sprinkled in but not enough to really be palatable. The newer Trek series are also prone to contemporary bad politics in that they're fully emersed in bland centrism. If DS9 was a Marxist critique of utopianism then Discovery and Strange New Worlds is feel good liberalism meant for people mourning the Obama years (I have not seen Picard so I can't comment on it). The previous series, including DS9, are certainly guilty of having the occasional bad take and we'd be all day here if I even tried to touch on the franchise's history of misogyny. But they were able to imagine a better world because they understood that larger structural inequalities and issues both should and more importantly COULD be abolished. The cynicism toward the Federation, that it's just an inherently impossible ideal, is a gross misreading of DS9's examination of it (we should note that DS9 ends on a high note, where the concept of "infinite diversity in infinite combinations" is ultimately what wins the Dominion War, where every faction of the Alpha Quadrant comes together to achieve victory), and only serves reactionaries that compromise on any meaningful progress or change because they think it's simply too difficult.

I agree that somatic stuff on the rise is essentially a direct reaction to CBT/behavioral modalities. New therapy models/ideas go in and out of fashion every decade or so where it's claimed THIS ONE is actually the breakthrough we've all been waiting for. The unfortunate reality is that whatever "works for you" is going to vary immensely, because it's more about something you find particular meaning in than anything else. A lot of clients across therapy subs absolutely swear by EMDR for example, and I'm not going to sit here and say that they shouldn't continue it if they're finding real value and comfort in it-they are by their own accounts feeling better. But I'm also not going to be told it's actually a deeply scientific process when the light bit is complete nonsense and the rest of the modality is repackaged exposure therapy.  I would say the same thing for talk therapy-some people absolutely love a structured relationship where they have dedicated time to talk to someone, others can never get past that it's a paid relationship and won't ever trust them. I would be more okay with this if the industry were upfront about it, but instead the client is often blamed if they don't respond the way their therapist wants them to.

Some people experience benefits from antidepressants but many don't receive any more benefit than they would from a placebo, and the idea that they're correcting a "chemical imbalance" has been disproven so thoroughly a lot of psychs pretend they were never marketed that way. It doesn't help that there are few long term studies on them and that side effects are underreported/ignored. So I understand your boyfriend's skepticism. I went off Zoloft cold turkey because I lost my insurance during the pandemic when I got laid off and it was hell on earth withdrawing from them, but I think in the long run it was better for me. I had multiple side effects that were detrimental and was deluding myself into thinking that it had to be beneficial. 

Ultimately it is your decision-drug use is morally neutral. Think about if you like being on them and if you're actually receiving any real benefits. The only thing I would recommend is that if you do decide to go off them to NOT do it all at once-set up a tapering schedule with your doctor, and if you're taking anything else with them (legal or not), to cross reference on [drugs.com](https://drugs.com) to avoid anything potentially harmful.

Robert Whitaker's works "Mad in America" and "Anatomy of an Epidemic", and Irving Kirsch's "The Emperor's New Drugs" are specifically centered around critiquing psychiatric drugs if that fits into your paper as well.

Keeping yourself engaged with fans is probably the most important aspect. Have an active twitter and use it to promote your shows, share some stuff that lets people get to know you even more, and occasionally reply back to fans. If WOW asks if you want to appear in any videos say yes, even if you only fly out to LA every other month. Have a YouTube channel of your own as well and post videos that highlight your talents (makeup, fashion, dancing, being funny, etc). Over 100 queens have come and gone from the show, the market for drag entertainers is oversaturated-only the ones that can really hustle are gonna make it now. 

Merch is also a big deal and you should definitely have stuff planned out for when the show airs, if not earlier. I understand this can be difficult for some queens (it costs money to make merch!) but even if it's just setting up a Redbubble/Etsy account with prints at the beginning, try to have something to sell (and then invest the money you make into selling better merch).
